blocks.text: Isaiah 40 begins the book’s 40–55 section in a practical reading map. Its opening announcement of comfort and return from Babylon uses creation and exodus imagery to portray a new homecoming, while not claiming that the effects of displacement or later conflict simply disappeared. The passage also moves among speakers and voices, so each speech should be identified from its immediate context rather than assumed to come from one speaker throughout. Ancient Greek Isaiah is itself an interpretive translation; its wording can reflect either a different Hebrew textual form or the translator’s own linguistic and theological decisions.

Mark 1:2–3 presents a composite citation from Exodus, Malachi, and Isaiah beneath an Isaiah heading, including Isaiah 40:3. This later use should be distinguished from questions about Isaiah 40’s own literary sense and historical referent; quotation, allusion, typology, and later Jewish or Christian reception are related but not identical interpretive claims.

The Great Isaiah Scroll is an almost complete manuscript witness to all sixty-six chapters of Isaiah. It broadly agrees with the Masoretic tradition while also containing many spelling and substantive differences; other Isaiah manuscripts and interpretive writings from Qumran likewise show that the book was actively copied and interpreted.
